Cookies are small text files that can be used by websites to make a user's experience more efficient.

The law states that we can store cookies on your device if they are strictly necessary for the operation of this site. For all other types of cookies we need your permission.

This site uses different types of cookies. Some cookies are placed by third party services that appear on our pages.

You can at any time change or withdraw your consent from the Cookie Declaration on our website.

Opinion/MAKING WAVES

The Chronology of Water is Kristen Stewart’s astonishing directorial debut

Kristen Stewart makes a wildly bold directorial debut with this fractured, feverish, and visually audacious portrait of trauma, memory, and survival.

By Luke Buckmaster|21 Aug 2026
Share
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:52
Instaread

You’ve never seen a film about a swimmer that’s anything like The Chronology of Water, the bold and visually audacious directorial debut of Kristen Stewart, adapted from a memoir by Lidia Yuknavitch. A sports movie this most certainly is not: there’s no big race to prepare for, no triumphant finish, or even a clear narrative trajectory. Swimming is one element in a fractured portrait of a woman trying to stay afloat, carrying profound trauma as she attends college, engages in an impetuous lifestyle of risk and drug-taking, and pursues a career as a writer. 

The Chronology of Water

2025
|
Dir: Kristen Stewart

From the outset, the film’s visual contours are sharp and jagged, trading in a savage kind of beauty. If this film is lyrical – one of those words critics are attracted to, like moths to the light – it’s a violent kind of lyricism: abrasive and uncomfortable, but somehow pretty, like colour-dyed sandpaper. You know that feeling, when your head is swimming with thoughts, not many of them good? Atmospherically, The Chronology of Water is a bit like that.

Early on, Lidia talks about her memory operating “as a series of fragments.” The film works that way too, conjuring oddly framed, mosaic-like visions that often focus on unexpected details, or common details in unexpected ways, making it initially difficult to grasp a clear sense of time and place. In other hands, this might’ve felt frustrating, like a pretentious student film. But in Stewart’s hands it’s a highly engaging synthesis of content and form: the story, and the shape of that story, fused to the emotional mindset of the protagonist. 

Gradually, the film’s visual discombobulation acquires narrative and emotional clarity. We learn that Lidia’s father sexually abuses her, and that she eventually leaves her Texas home for college, where her ambitions as a swimmer are quickly overtaken by drugs, sex and partying. She’s impetuous and self-destructive, making big decisions haphazardly, including marrying fellow student Phillip (Earl Cave) soon after meeting him.

She attends writing class, around midway through the runtime, and meets a charmingly dishevelled teacher, One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest author Ken Kesey (Jim Belushi). These moments, in which he implores his students to “write bizarre sentences,” feels like a reprieve: a more pleasant counter to the film’s frenetic first half. You can also sense that these quieter moments aren’t going to last forever.

Stewart continues to find ways to visually communicate that while people can leave a location, move on from a geographical place, they can never move on from themselves; you can’t outrun your own feet. “Memories are stories,” Lidia says, “so you better come up with one you can live with.” This line reflects how Stewart views memories: as something felt – and continuously remade – rather than recalled.

On a human level, Imogen Poots’ portrayal of Lidia is the glue binding the film together. And by god she can act: this is an awesome, heady performance, sensual and intoxicating, complex and difficult to pin down. The enigmatic look in her eyes seems to deepen and intensify as the story progresses, suggesting that the journey of getting to know the protagonist is partly making her more of a stranger: adding detail while exposing other areas to explore, new spaces in her psyche to comprehend. 

The Chronology of Water‘s emotional currents feel so forceful, so much like a whirlwind, it’s a wonder Poots can even stand up. Stewart’s electrically immersive film – one of the best of 2026 – can be intellectualised, to some degree, but like entering water, like submerging yourself in the ocean, it can only really be experienced. You feel it, and you feel it hard. 

Luke Buckmaster
Luke Buckmaster is chief film and TV critic of Flicks.
